cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: The European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) was drafted in 1950 by the Council of Europe in response to the atrocities of the Second World War

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: The UK ratified the ECHR in 1951 and accepted the right of individual petition to the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) in 1966

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: The Human Rights Act 1998 incorporated the rights from the ECHR into UK domestic law, coming into force on 2 October 2000

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Section 2 of the HRA 1998 requires UK courts to take into account judgments of the ECtHR when interpreting Convention rights

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Section 3 of the HRA 1998 requires legislation to be read and given effect in a way compatible with Convention rights so far as it is possible to do so

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Section 4 of the HRA 1998 allows courts to issue a declaration of incompatibility if primary legislation cannot be read compatibly with Convention rights

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Section 6 of the HRA 1998 makes it unlawful for a public authority to act in a way incompatible with a Convention right

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Key Convention rights include: Article 2 (right to life), Article 3 (prohibition of torture), Article 5 (right to liberty), Article 6 (right to a fair trial)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Further rights include Article 8 (right to private and family life), Article 9 (freedom of thought, conscience and religion), Article 10 (freedom of expression) and Article 11 (freedom of assembly)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Convention rights are not absolute: most are qualified (can be restricted if necessary and proportionate) or limited (can be restricted in defined circumstances)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: Article 3 and Article 4 are absolute rights that can never be restricted under any circumstances

cards.front: Recall a key point about Human Rights & the ECHR
cards.back: The HRA 1998 does not give courts power to strike down primary legislation; Parliament remains sovereign and can legislate inconsistently with Convention rights

cards.front: What should you know about gcse law exam tips — human rights & the echr?
cards.back: 1. For Human Rights & the ECHR questions, identify the relevant area of law and state the legal principles clearly 2. Apply legal rules to the facts of the scenario — don't just state the law 3. When evaluating, consider both the effectiveness and fairness of legal rules 4. Reference relevant cases and statutes when discussing Human Rights & the ECHR 5. Consider reform proposals and alternative approaches where relevant
